title: Automatic Multimodal UX Improvement Recommendations from LLM Agent User Simulations
abstract: The authors propose AMUSER, a multimodal LLM-agent framework that simulates realistic users on live websites and turns the simulation traces into prioritised, ranked UX improvement recommendations. On commercial websites, AMUSER substantially outperforms text-only simulation on ranking quality while reducing simulation cost by 89%.

title: Agent and Tool Search: Foundations, Techniques, and Open Challenges
BiasTrace: Linking Reasoning Behaviours to Biased Outputs in LLMs
abstract: The authors introduce BiasTrace, a fine-grained annotation scheme that links LLM reasoning behaviours to biased outputs, applied at scale via a validated LLM-as-a-judge. They find biased outputs often stem from subtle reasoning behaviours rather than explicitly biased language, and that reasoning-level annotations improve bias detection and can support inference-time mitigation.

title: InnoEval: On Research Idea Evaluation as a Knowledge-Grounded, Multi-Perspective Reasoning Problem
abstract: The authors frame research idea evaluation as a knowledge-grounded, multi-perspective reasoning problem and introduce InnoEval, combining a knowledge search engine over papers, web pages and code with a panel of reviewer personas reaching consensus across decoupled scoring dimensions.

venue: ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)
title: Auto-Judge: A Cross-Task Benchmark for Comparing LLM Judges for Citation-Grounded RAG Systems
When AI Benchmarks Plateau: A Systematic Study of Benchmark Saturation
abstract: The authors define benchmark saturation as the loss of reliable discriminative power among top-performing models and study it across 60 LLM benchmarks using 14 design properties, finding nearly half are saturated and that resistance depends more on expert curation than on whether test data is public.

title: Beyond Output Critique: Self-Correction via Task Distillation
abstract: The authors argue most self-correction methods patch surface errors at the output level without fixing deeper reasoning flaws, and propose SELF-THOUGHT, which adds an intermediate task-abstraction step before solution refinement, helping smaller models self-correct more reliably.

venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
title: Automated Rubrics for Reliable Evaluation of Medical Dialogue Systems
abstract: The authors propose a retrieval-augmented multi-agent system that generates instance-specific evaluation rubrics for medical dialogue from decomposed medical evidence and user interaction constraints, improving discriminative power over a GPT-4o baseline on HealthBench.

venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
title: AgentCoMa: A Compositional Benchmark Mixing Commonsense and Mathematical Reasoning in Real-World Scenarios
abstract: AgentCoMa pairs a commonsense reasoning step with an elementary math step in each task. Across 61 LLMs, models handle each reasoning type well in isolation but accuracy drops by nearly 30% on average when the steps must be combined.

title: Interplay: Training Independent Simulators for Reference-Free Conversational Recommendation
abstract: Instead of using a single LLM to write whole conversations around a predetermined target item, the authors train two independent simulators, one playing the user and one the recommender, that converse without a fixed target, matching or exceeding existing simulation methods.

title: Self-Correcting Large Language Models: Generation vs. Multiple Choice
abstract: The authors compare self-correction behaviour across open-ended generation and multiple-choice settings, finding free-form generation benefits from re-interpretation and compositional refinement while multiple-choice selection is capped by the provided options.

title: Who Evaluates AI's Social Impacts? Mapping Coverage and Gaps in First and Third Party Evaluations
abstract: The authors analyze first-party foundation model release reports alongside third-party evaluation sources and developer interviews to map who evaluates AI's social impacts, finding first-party reporting is often thin while outside researchers provide more thorough coverage of bias and harm.

venue: Workshop on Large Language Models for Evaluation in Information Retrieval, co-located with SIGIR
title: LLM4Eval: Large Language Model for Evaluation in IR
Beyond Internal Data: Bounding and Estimating Fairness from Incomplete Data
abstract: Fairness-relevant data is often split across separate sources that each only give partial, marginal information. The authors estimate the set of all joint distributions consistent with the observed marginals, letting them bound and estimate fairness metrics even when protected attributes are missing from the model's input data.

title: PREF: Reference-Free Evaluation of Personalised Text Generation in LLMs
abstract: PREF evaluates personalised text generation in three stages: a coverage stage generates a query-specific guideline of quality criteria, a preference stage adapts it to the target user, and a scoring stage has an LLM judge rate candidates against the resulting rubric, improving accuracy and calibration over strong baselines.

venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
title: Towards Understanding Bias in Synthetic Data for Evaluation
abstract: The authors investigate the reliability of LLM-generated synthetic test collections for IR evaluation, finding that bias in synthetic test collections can meaningfully affect absolute system performance estimates, though its effect on relative system comparisons is smaller.

venue: Workshop on Large Language Models for Evaluation in Information Retrieval, co-located with WSDM
title: LLM4Eval@WSDM 2025: Large Language Model for Evaluation in Information Retrieval

venue: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference (WWW)
title: Judging the Judges: A Collection of LLM-Generated Relevance Judgements
abstract: The authors report on the LLMJudge challenge, run as part of the LLM4Eval workshop at SIGIR 2024, which released and evaluated 42 sets of LLM-generated relevance labels for the TREC 2023 Deep Learning track produced by eight participating teams, probing systematic biases and comparing LLMs with human assessors.

venue: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference (WWW)
title: JudgeBlender: Ensembling Judgments for Automatic Relevance Assessment
abstract: JudgeBlender combines relevance judgments across multiple smaller, open-source LLMs or multiple prompts instead of relying on a single large, expensive model like GPT-4. Evaluated on the LLMJudge benchmark, it achieves competitive performance, showing very large models are often unnecessary for reliable relevance assessment.

venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
title: Empirical Analysis on User Profile in Personalized LLMs
abstract: Utilizing user profiles to personalize Large Language Models (LLMs) has been shown to enhance the performance on a wide range of tasks. However, the precise role of user profiles and their effect mechanism on LLMs remains unclear. This study first confirms that the effectiveness of user profiles is primarily due to personalization information rather than semantic information. Furthermore, we investigate how user profiles affect the personalization of LLMs. Within the user profile, we reveal that it is the historical personalized response produced or approved by users that plays a pivotal role in personalizing LLMs. This discovery unlocks the potential of LLMs to incorporate a greater number of user profiles within the constraints of limited input length. As for the position of user profiles, we observe that user profiles integrated into different positions of the input context do not contribute equally to personalization. Instead, where the user profile that is closer to the beginning affects more on the personalization of LLMs.
note: Published as a short paper at ACM CIKM 2025.

title: SynDL: A Large-Scale Synthetic Test Collection for Passage Retrieval
Report on the 1st Workshop on Large Language Model for Evaluation in Information Retrieval (LLM4Eval 2024) at SIGIR 2024
abstract: The first edition of the workshop on Large Language Model for Evaluation in Information Retrieval (LLM4Eval 2024) took place in July 2024, co-located with the ACM SIGIR Conference 2024 in the USA (SIGIR 2024). The aim was to bring information retrieval researchers together around the topic of LLMs for evaluation in information retrieval that gathered attention with the advancement of large language models and generative AI. Given the novelty of the topic, the workshop was focused around multi-sided discussions, namely panels and poster sessions of the accepted proceedings papers.

title: LLMJudge: LLMs for Relevance Judgments

venue: ACM SIGIR International Conference on Theory of Information Retrieval (ICTIR)
title: Personalized Beyond-accuracy Calibration in Recommendation
abstract: Recommender systems usually aim to optimize accuracy in a supervised setting. Due to various data biases, they often fail to enhance other critical qualities that go beyond accuracy, such as diversity, novelty, and serendipity. In this work, we take a user-centric approach and demonstrate that users have distinct preferences for beyond-accuracy metrics. We propose a post-ranking greedy optimization algorithm that ensures recommendations are not only accurate but also meet users' beyond-accuracy preferences.

venue: ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)
title: LLM4Eval: Large Language Model for Evaluation in IR
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated increasing task-solving abilities not present in smaller models. Utilizing the capabilities and responsibilities of LLMs for automated evaluation (LLM4Eval) has recently attracted considerable attention in multiple research communities. The main goal of the LLM4Eval workshop is to bring together researchers from industry and academia to discuss various aspects of LLMs for evaluation in information retrieval, including automated judgments, retrieval-augmented generation pipeline evaluation, altering human evaluation, robustness, and trustworthiness of LLMs for evaluation.

venue: ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)
title: Synthetic Test Collections for Retrieval Evaluation
abstract: Test collections play a vital role in evaluation of information retrieval (IR) systems. Obtaining a diverse set of user queries for test collection construction can be challenging, and acquiring relevance judgments is often costly and resource-intensive. In this paper, we comprehensively investigate whether it is possible to use LLMs to construct fully synthetic test collections by generating not only synthetic judgments but also synthetic queries. In particular, we analyse whether it is possible to construct reliable synthetic test collections and the potential risks of bias such test collections may exhibit towards LLM-based models. Our experiments indicate that using LLMs it is possible to construct synthetic test collections that can reliably be used for retrieval evaluation.

title: A Personalized Framework for Consumer and Producer Group Fairness Optimization in Recommender Systems
abstract: We propose CP-FairRank, an optimization-based re-ranking algorithm that seamlessly integrates fairness constraints from both the consumer and producer side in a joint objective framework. Through large-scale experiments on eight datasets and four mainstream collaborative filtering recommendation models, we demonstrate that our proposed strategy is able to improve both consumer and producer fairness without compromising overall recommendation quality.

venue: Findings of the European Chapter of the ACL (EACL)
title: Clarifying the Path to User Satisfaction: An Investigation into Clarification Usefulness
abstract: Clarifying questions are an integral component of modern information retrieval systems, directly impacting user satisfaction and overall system performance. This research addresses the need to identify and leverage key features that contribute to the classification of clarifying questions. Our empirical results provide three main insights into the qualities of effective query clarification: (1) specific questions are more effective than generic ones; (2) the subjectivity and emotional tone of a question play a role; and (3) shorter and more ambiguous queries benefit significantly from clarification.

venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
title: Transparent and Scrutable Recommendations Using Natural Language User Profiles
abstract: The authors use an LLM to write a natural-language profile of a user's preferences from their past reviews, then fine-tune an LLM to predict ratings using only this readable text profile instead of opaque embeddings. Editing the profile directly changes the resulting recommendations.

venue: Algorithmic Fairness through the Lens of Metrics and Evaluation Workshop, co-located with NeurIPS
title: Beyond Internal Data: Constructing Complete Datasets for Fairness Testing
abstract: The authors propose leveraging separate, overlapping incomplete datasets to construct a complete synthetic dataset that includes demographic information missing from an institution's internal data alone, enabling more thorough fairness testing.

title: Provider Fairness and Beyond-Accuracy Trade-offs in Recommender Systems

venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
title: A Survey on Asking Clarification Questions Datasets in Conversational Systems
abstract: The ability to understand a user's underlying needs is critical for conversational systems, especially with limited input from users in a conversation. Thus, Asking Clarification Questions (ACQs) to reveal users' true intent from their queries or utterances arise as an essential task. A key limitation of existing ACQs studies is their incomparability, from inconsistent use of data, distinct experimental setups and evaluation strategies. In this paper we comprehensively analyse the current ACQs research status, offering a detailed comparison of publicly available datasets, and discuss the applied evaluation metrics, joined with benchmarks for multiple ACQs-related tasks.

title: When and What to Ask Through World States and Text Instructions: IGLU NLP Challenge Solution
abstract: In collaborative building, builders may encounter situations that are difficult to interpret based on the available information and instructions, leading to ambiguity. In the NeurIPS 2022 Competition NLP Task, we address two key research questions: when should the agent ask for clarification, and what clarification questions should it ask? For the classification task, our model achieves an F1 score of 0.757, which placed 3rd on the leaderboard. For the ranking task, our model achieves about 0.38 for Mean Reciprocal Rank.

venue: Pacific-Asia Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (PAKDD)
title: Quantifying the Bias of Transformer-Based Language Models for African American English in Masked Language Modeling
abstract: We propose and thoroughly validate an evaluation technique to assess the quality and bias of language model predictions on transcripts of both spoken African American English (AAE) and Spoken American English (SAE). Our analysis reveals the presence of a bias towards SAE encoded by state-of-the-art LMs such as BERT and DistilBERT and a lower bias in distilled LMs.

title: LLM-based Retrieval and Generation Pipelines for TREC Interactive Knowledge Assistance Track (iKAT) 2023
abstract: The team compares retrieve-then-generate and generate-then-retrieve pipelines for TREC iKAT 2023. Their generate-then-retrieve approach, using GPT-4 to draft an initial answer turned into BM25 queries and reranked with MiniLM, outperformed their other automatic runs on passage ranking.

title: Overview of the TREC 2023 Deep Learning Track
abstract: The official overview of the fifth year of the TREC Deep Learning track, built on the MS MARCO v2 passage and document collections, focused on building reusable, complete test collections, including experiments evaluating with LLM-synthesised queries alongside human-written ones.

venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP
title: Improving Conversational Recommendation Systems via Bias Analysis and Language-Model-Enhanced Data Augmentation
abstract: The authors analyze feedback-loop biases in conversational recommender benchmarks and propose two LLM-based data augmentation strategies, Once-Aug and PopNudge, which give consistent gains on the ReDial and TG-ReDial benchmarks.

venue: Theory of Mind in Communicating Agents Workshop, co-located with ICML
title: Do LLMs Selectively Encode the Goal of an Agent's Reach?
abstract: The authors test whether LLMs show an early Theory-of-Mind-like bias toward treating the object, rather than the location, as the goal of an agent's reach. Two models show a selective bias for purposeful agents, but it differs from humans' and is fragile to equivalent prompt variations.

title: CAPRI: Context-aware Point-of-Interest Recommendation Framework
abstract: CAPRI is an open-source framework for context-aware POI recommendation that integrates models such as GeoSoCa, LORE and USG with a strategy for fusing contextual information, and evaluates beyond accuracy with novelty, personalization, diversity and fairness metrics.

title: Towards Asking Clarification Questions for Information Seeking on Task-Oriented Dialogues
abstract: The authors propose MAS2S, a Multi-Attention Seq2Seq Network that asks clarifying questions about both a user's information need and their profile in task-oriented dialogue, and extend an existing dataset into ClariT (~100k dialogues).

venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
title: Towards Confidence-Aware Calibrated Recommendation
abstract: Calibration ensures that the distribution of recommended item categories is consistent with the user's historical data. This work presents a set of properties that address various aspects of a desired calibrated recommender system, and proposes a confidence-aware optimization-based re-ranking algorithm to find the balance between calibration, relevance, and item diversity, while simultaneously accounting for calibration confidence based on user profile size.

title: Exploring the Impact of Temporal Bias in Point-of-Interest Recommendation
abstract: This paper examines the effect of temporal bias, defined as the difference between users' check-in hours, leisure vs. work hours, on the consumer-side fairness of context-aware recommendation algorithms. The findings show that the examined context-aware recommendation models prefer one group of users over another based on the time of check-in and that this preference persists even when users have the same amount of interactions.

title: PyCPFair: A Framework for Consumer and Producer Fairness in Recommender Systems
abstract: This paper presents PyCPFair, a Python-based framework for consumer and producer fairness in recommender systems. The ease-of-use and flexibility of the presented framework have allowed reducing the development time and increased evaluation strategies of fairness models for recommender systems.

title: The Role of Context Fusion on Accuracy, Beyond-Accuracy, and Fairness of Point-of-Interest Recommendation Systems
abstract: In this work, we propose a linear regression-based fusion of POI contexts that effectively finds the best combination of contexts for each user, or group of users, from their historical interactions. Our study suggests that appropriate context fusion is an essential element of an accurate, fair, and transparent POI recommendation system.

venue: ACM Conference on User Modeling, Adaptation and Personalization (UMAP)
title: ViralBERT: A User Focused BERT-Based Approach to Virality Prediction
abstract: In this paper we propose ViralBERT, which can be used to predict the virality of tweets using content- and user-based features. We collect a dataset of 330k tweets to train ViralBERT and validate the efficacy of our model using baselines from current studies in this field. Our experiments show that our approach outperforms these baselines, with a 13% increase in both F1 Score and Accuracy compared to the best performing baseline method.

venue: ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)
title: Experiments on Generalizability of User-Oriented Fairness in Recommender Systems
abstract: In this paper, we re-produce a user-oriented fairness study and provide extensive experiments to analyze the dependency of their proposed method on various fairness and recommendation aspects, including the recommendation domain, nature of the base ranking model, and user grouping method. We discover interesting trends and trade-offs between the model's performance in terms of different evaluation metrics.

venue: ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR)
title: CPFair: Personalized Consumer and Producer Fairness Re-Ranking for Recommender Systems
abstract: In this work, we present an optimization-based re-ranking approach that seamlessly integrates fairness constraints from both the consumer and producer-side in a joint objective framework. We demonstrate through large-scale experiments on 8 datasets that our proposed method is capable of improving both consumer and producer fairness without reducing overall recommendation quality.

venue: Workshop on Algorithmic Bias in Search and Recommendation (ECIR)
title: The Unfairness of Popularity Bias in Book Recommendation
abstract: We analyze the well-known Book-Crossing dataset and define three user groups based on their tendency towards popular items (Niche, Diverse, Bestseller-focused). Our results indicate that most state-of-the-art recommendation algorithms suffer from popularity bias in the book domain, and fail to meet users' expectations with Niche and Diverse tastes despite having a larger profile size.

venue: Workshop on Algorithmic Bias in Search and Recommendation (ECIR)
title: The Unfairness of Active Users and Popularity Bias in Point-of-Interest Recommendation
abstract: This paper studies the interplay between (i) the unfairness of active users, (ii) the unfairness of popular items, and (iii) the accuracy of recommendation as three angles of our study triangle. Experimental validation of eight different recommendation models on two publicly available POI datasets indicates that most well-performing models suffer seriously from the unfairness of popularity bias.

title: A Systematic Analysis on the Impact of Contextual Information on Point-of-Interest Recommendation
abstract: In this paper, we propose different contextual models and analyze the fusion of different major contextual information in POI recommendation. Our results indicate that while modeling geographical and temporal influences can improve recommendation quality, fusing all other contextual information into a recommendation model is not always the best strategy.

title: Leveraging Social Influence Based on Users Activity Centers for Point-of-Interest Recommendation
abstract: In this paper, we address data sparsity by incorporating social, geographical, and temporal information into the Matrix Factorization technique. Our ablation study shows that the social model improves the performance of our proposed POI recommendation system by 31% and 14% on the Gowalla and Yelp datasets in terms of Precision@10.

venue: CSCW Workshop on Investigating and Mitigating Biases in Crowdsourced Data (BCD)
title: Demographic Biases of Crowd Workers in Key Opinion Leaders Finding
abstract: Data collected through crowdsourcing is affected by the inherent demographic biases of crowd workers. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective approach based on demographic information of candidate Key Opinion Leaders and their counterfactual value.

title: Joint Geographical and Temporal Modeling Based on Matrix Factorization for Point-of-Interest Recommendation
abstract: We perform a study on user mobility patterns where we find that users' check-ins happen around several centers depending on their current temporal state. We propose a spatio-temporal activity-centers algorithm, STACP, to model users' behavior more accurately. Experimental results on Gowalla and Foursquare show a statistically significant performance improvement compared to the state of the art.

title: Mining Shape of Expertise: A Novel Approach Based on Convolutional Neural Network
abstract: The authors address T-shaped expert finding, detecting and ranking people with a broad knowledge base plus one deep specialty, using a CNN model with two parallel branches that extract latent vectors of users and queries to match queries with experts on Stack Overflow.

venue: ACM SIGIR International Conference on Theory of Information Retrieval (ICTIR)
title: Category-Aware Location Embedding for Point-of-Interest Recommendation
LGLMF: Local Geographical based Logistic Matrix Factorization Model for POI Recommendation
abstract: The authors model a user's main region of activity and the relevance of each location within it, then fuse this local geographical model into Logistic Matrix Factorization for POI recommendation, outperforming other state-of-the-art POI recommendation methods on two well-known datasets.

title: A Regression Approach to Movie Rating Prediction using Multimedia Content and Metadata
abstract: The team treats movie rating prediction (average rating, rating standard deviation and number of ratings) as a regression problem using audio and visual trailer features plus metadata, comparing ridge regression, support vector regression and shallow/deep neural networks.

title: A Short Review on Point-of-Interest Recommender Systems

venue: National Conference on Distributed Computing and Big Data Processing (DCBDP)
title: A Study of Recent Contributions on Information Extraction
Comparison of Tumor and Normal Cells Protein-Protein Interaction Network Parameters
abstract: In this paper, we compared cancerous and normal cells according to their protein-protein interaction network. The experimental results show that Graph Degree Mean, Subgraph Centrality, Betweenness, and Hubs have higher values in the cancer cells and can be used as a measure to distinguish between normal and cancerous networks.

venue: BSc Thesis, University of Zanjan (in Persian)
title: Natural and Cancer Cells Detection Using Analysis of Protein Interaction Networks
